fixes.explanation: Yes, ankle-deep. The man measures off a thousand cubits and leads Ezekiel through ankle-deep water (Ezekiel 47:3). It's the shallowest stretch of the walk, and the water only gets deeper from here.

I get the guess, since smoke is something I know plenty about from my ovens. But Ezekiel says he saw water flowing from under the threshold of the temple toward the east (Ezekiel 47:1). Water is what he sees coming out, friend. In my bakery, I'd take that over smoke any day.

That's quite a jump, friend. After the first thousand cubits, the text says the man led Ezekiel through ankle-deep water (Ezekiel 47:3). Chest-deep isn't one of the depths in the walk. The water goes ankle, knee, then waist (Ezekiel 47:4).

Whoa, slow down, friend. After the first thousand cubits it's only ankle-deep (Ezekiel 47:3). Neck-deep isn't one of the depths Ezekiel wades through. He goes through ankle, knee and waist-deep water, and then comes to a river that could not be crossed on foot (Ezekiel 47:4-5).
Chin-deep is quite a leap, friend. After the knees, the next stretch is waist-deep water (Ezekiel 47:4). Chin isn't a depth the text gives. Waist is where the man leads him.

Tents make sense for a riverbank, but that's not what Ezekiel sees. The text says that when he arrived, he saw a great number of trees along both banks of the river (Ezekiel 47:7). Trees are what he reports, friend, not tents.

That's a big image, friend, but the text has a different one. Ezekiel says that when he arrived, he saw a great number of trees along both banks of the river (Ezekiel 47:7). Trees on both banks is what he sees, and a great number of them.

I see why you'd think so, since the Dead Sea doesn't sound like a lively spot. But the man says that when the river empties into it, the water there becomes fresh (Ezekiel 47:8). Fresh is the word he uses, friend. The water changes, and it doesn't dry up.

That's a dramatic guess, friend, but the text goes another way. The man says that when the river empties into the Dead Sea, the water there becomes fresh (Ezekiel 47:8). Fresh water is the result he names, and that's good news.

Two is a start, but this river is overachieving. The man says the fishermen will catch "…fish of many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea." (Ezekiel 47:10) That's a lot more than a pair. Many kinds, friend.

Salt is right. The man says the swamps and marshes will not become fresh, and "they will be left for salt." (Ezekiel 47:11) Even with everything else flourishing where the river flows, that's what he says about those spots. Salt, friend.

Grazing makes sense for open land, friend, but that's not what the man says. He says the swamps and marshes will not become fresh, and "they will be left for salt." (Ezekiel 47:11) Salt is the use he names for them.

Good thought for a place with water, friend, but the man says something else. The swamps and marshes will not become fresh, and "they will be left for salt." (Ezekiel 47:11) Salt is what he names, not farming.

I can see why that might sound right, since leaves wither all the time. But the man says the opposite: "Their leaves will not wither, and their fruit will not fail." (Ezekiel 47:12) These trees don't follow the usual leaf rules, friend.
That's right, it's false. The man says, "Their leaves will not wither, and their fruit will not fail." (Ezekiel 47:12) No withering for the leaves, friend. And the fruit will not fail either.

Fishermen hauling buckets would be a lot of work, friend. But the man never says that. He says the trees bear fruit each month "…because the water from the sanctuary flows to them." (Ezekiel 47:12) That's the reason he gives.

Weaving is a good use for leaves, friend, but it's not what the man says. He says, "Their fruit will be used for food and their leaves for healing." (Ezekiel 47:12) So the leaves are for healing, not weaving.
